claim: Eukaryotic DNA is highly organized within nuclei and this organization is important for genome function.
source: Eukaryotic DNA is highly organized within nuclei and this organization is important for genome function.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about eukaryotic genome organization.

claim: Fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) approaches allow 3D architectures of genomes to be visualized.
source: Fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) approaches allow 3D architectures of genomes to be visualized.
evidence: This is established knowledge about FISH technology capabilities.

claim: The described multiplexed DNA FISH Oligopaint library targets the entire Caenorhabditis elegans genome at chromosome, three megabase, and 500 kb scales.
source: Here, we describe a multiplexed DNA FISH Oligopaint library that targets the entire Caenorhabditis elegans genome at chromosome, three megabase, and 500 kb scales.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the library design described in the manuscript, supported by the experimental data and figures showing the library structure.

claim: The hybridization strategy couples a single primary probe synthesis reaction to dye conjugated detection oligos via bridge oligos.
source: We describe a hybridization strategy that provides flexibility to DNA FISH experiments by coupling a single primary probe synthesis reaction to dye conjugated detection oligos via bridge oligos, eliminating the time and cost typically associated with labeling probe sets for individual experiments.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach developed in the study, supported by the methods and results.

claim: The approach allows visualization of genome organization at varying scales in all/most cells across all stages of development in an intact animal model system.
source: The approach allows visualization of genome organization at varying scales in all/most cells across all stages of development in an intact animal model system.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing FISH in various cell types and developmental stages.

claim: The basic unit of genome organization is the nucleosome.
source: The basic unit of genome organization is the nucleosome.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about chromatin structure.

claim: Nucleosomes assemble into higher order structures whose biogenesis, maintenance, regulation, and purpose are poorly understood.
source: Nucleosomes assemble into higher order structures whose biogenesis, maintenance, regulation, and purpose are poorly understood (Bickmore, 2013; Bonev and Cavalli, 2016; Meaburn, 2016; Yu and Ren, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: DNA fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) technologies and chromatin conformation capture techniques allow 3D architectures of genomes to be assessed.
source: DNA fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) technologies and chromatin conformation capture techniques allow 3D architectures of genomes to be assessed (Bauman et al., 1980; Beliveau et al., 2012; Bienko et al., 2013; Dekker et al., 2013, Dekker et al., 2002; Lieberman-Aiden et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: Many eukaryotic genomes are assembled into megabase-sized structures termed topologically associated domains (TADs).
source: For instance, chromatin capture experiments show that many eukaryotic genomes are assembled into megabase-sized structures termed topologically associated domains (TADs).
evidence: This is established knowledge from chromatin capture experiments.

claim: TADs and larger organizational units termed compartments are thought to allow subregions of chromosomes to share and integrate long-range transcriptional regulatory signals.
source: TADs, and larger organizational units termed compartments, are thought to allow subregions of chromosomes to share and integrate long-range transcriptional regulatory signals (Dekker and Heard, 2015; Dekker and Mirny, 2016; Dixon et al., 2012; Lieberman-Aiden et al., 2009; Vernimmen and Bickmore, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature and represents current scientific understanding.

claim: Active genes tend to localize near nuclear pores and/or the nuclear interior while inactive genes tend to localize to the nuclear periphery, distant from nuclear pores.
source: Additionally, DNA FISH and chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) experiments have shown that the position of genes within nuclei is often not random: active genes tend to localize near nuclear pores and/or the nuclear interior while inactive genes tend to localize to the nuclear periphery, distant from nuclear pores (Casolari et al., 2004; Gonzalez-Sandoval and Gasser, 2016; Lemaître and Bickmore, 2015; Pickersgill et al., 2006; van Steensel and Belmont, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: Individual chromosomes tend to occupy distinct non-overlapping regions of subnuclear space, even in interphase nuclei (termed chromosome territories).
source: Finally, DNA FISH experiments have shown that individual chromosomes tend to occupy distinct non-overlapping regions of subnuclear space, even in interphase nuclei (termed chromosome territories) (Bolzer et al., 2005; Cremer and Cremer, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: C. elegans is an excellent model for studying genome organization in an intact animal due to its size (1 mm), lifespan (~3 days to reproductive maturity), genome size (100 Mb across five autosomes and one sex chromosome), and transparent body.
source: The nematode Caenorhabditis elegans is an excellent model for studying genome organization in an intact animal due to its size (1 mm), lifespan (~3 days to reproductive maturity), genome size (100 Mb across five autosomes and one sex chromosome), and transparent body.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans as a model organism.

claim: A previous chromosome level DNA FISH experiment in C. elegans used 127 yeast artificial chromosome (YAC) clones split into 50 amplification reactions for three chromosome probe generation.
source: For example, a previous chromosome level DNA FISH experiment in C. elegans used 127 yeast artificial chromosome (YAC) clones split into 50 amplification reactions for three chromosome probe generation (Nabeshima et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: Oligopaint technology has made DNA FISH probe production faster, cheaper, and more flexible.
source: Oligopaint technology has made DNA FISH probe production faster, cheaper, and more flexible (Beliveau et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: Oligopaint takes advantage of massively parallel DNA synthesis technologies to create user defined libraries containing hundreds of thousands of individual DNA oligos each comprised of a short (42 bp) DNA sequence that hybridizes to a genome, as well as additional 'barcode' sequences.
source: Oligopaint takes advantage of massively parallel DNA synthesis technologies to create user defined libraries containing hundreds of thousands of individual DNA oligos each comprised of a short (42 bp) DNA sequence that hybridizes to a genome, as well as additional 'barcode' sequences that serve two major functions.
evidence: This describes the Oligopaint technology, supported by citations.

claim: Barcodes allow probes to be repeatedly amplified from an Oligopaint library, thus providing a virtually inexhaustible supply of oligos for DNA FISH.
source: First, barcodes allow probes to be repeatedly amplified from an Oligopaint library, thus providing a virtually inexhaustible supply of oligos for DNA FISH (Beliveau et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2015; Murgha et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Barcodes allow pre-labeled detection oligos to be used to detect Oligopaint oligos, thus obviating the need for fluorescently labeling probes for each DNA FISH experiment.
source: Second, barcodes allow pre-labeled detection oligos to be used to detect Oligopaint oligos, thus obviating the need for fluorescently labeling probes for each DNA FISH experiment (Beliveau et al., 2015; Beliveau et al., 2012; Nir et al., 2018; Rosin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: The Oligopaint technology has been used to visualize chromosome territories in Drosophila cultured cells in normal and mutant contexts.
source: Previously, the Oligopaint technology has been used to visualize chromosome territories in Drosophila cultured cells in normal and mutant contexts (Rosin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: The bioinformatics pipeline identified approximately nine suitable probe sequences per kilobase of C. elegans genomic DNA.
source: The results of our bioinformatic search revealed approximately nine suitable probe sequences per kilobase of C. elegans genomic DNA (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Table 1.

claim: The generated Oligopaint library contained, on average, ~2 probe sequences per kb of genomic DNA across each C. elegans chromosome.
source: We generated an Oligopaint library that contained, on average,~2 probe sequences per kb of genomic DNA across each C. elegans chromosome (Figure 1a and Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 1a and Table 1.

claim: Few gaps between probes exceeded 5 kb (33 out of 25,174), with the largest gap spanning ~18 kb for chromosome I.
source: Few gaps between probes exceeded 5 kb (33 out of 25,174), with the largest gap spanning ~18 kb.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of the probe distribution data.

claim: A subtle decrease in probe density is observed on chromosome arms, perhaps due to an increase in repetitive sequences in these regions.
source: A subtle decrease in probe density is observed on chromosome arms, perhaps due to an increase in repetitive sequences in these regions, which biased against probe selection (C. elegans C. elegans Sequencing Consortium, 1998).
evidence: This is an inference based on observed data and supported by a citation about C. elegans genome structure.

claim: The library consisted of 170,594 oligos (termed primary Oligopaint oligos).
source: In total, the library consisted of 170,594 oligos (termed primary Oligopaint oligos), which each contain 42 bp of unique genomic sequence flanked by barcode sequences that allow for DNA FISH targeting each of the six C. elegans chromosomes, as well as three megabase, or 500 kb subregions of these chromosomes (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by the library design data.

claim: Bridge oligos provide versatility (and cost savings) to DNA FISH experiments as these oligos allow any primary probe set to be coupled to any detection probe set with minimal additional cost.
source: Bridge oligos provide versatility (and cost savings) to DNA FISH experiments as these oligos allow any primary probe set to be coupled to any detection probe set with minimal additional cost.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the advantages of the bridge oligo strategy.

claim: By using detection oligos with fluorophores on both 3' and 5' termini, two detection oligos per bridge oligo, and bridge oligos that target the 5' and 3' barcode sequence of primary probes, it is possible to have each primary oligo recognized by eight fluorophores.
source: By using 1) detection oligos with fluorophores on both 3' and 5' termini, 2) two detection oligos per bridge oligo, and 3) bridge oligos that target the 5' and 3' barcode sequence of primary probes, it is possible to have each primary oligo recognized by eight fluorophores.
evidence: This is an inference based on the design of the detection system.

claim: Chromosome II DNA FISH stained a single bivalent in wild-type oocytes (58/58).
source: As expected, X chromosome DNA FISH stained a single bivalent in wild-type oocytes (58/58) and two univalents in 84% of him-8 oocytes (51/61) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and quantification.

claim: X chromosome DNA FISH stained two univalents in 84% of him-8 oocytes (51/61).
source: As expected, X chromosome DNA FISH stained a single bivalent in wild-type oocytes (58/58) and two univalents in 84% of him-8 oocytes (51/61) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and quantification.

claim: HIM-8 is required for X chromosome homolog pairing during meiosis.
source: HIM-8 is required for X chromosome homolog pairing during meiosis and, consequently, X chromosomes are present as two univalents (and not a single bivalent) in him-8 mutant animals (Phillips et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: X chromosomes are present as two univalents (and not a single bivalent) in him-8 mutant animals.
source: HIM-8 is required for X chromosome homolog pairing during meiosis and, consequently, X chromosomes are present as two univalents (and not a single bivalent) in him-8 mutant animals (Phillips et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the literature and confirmed by experimental data.

claim: The C. elegans Oligopaint library is specific.
source: Together the data show that the C. elegans Oligopaint library is specific.
evidence: This is supported by multiple experimental observations showing expected staining patterns.

claim: 83% of larval stage animals (1085/1303) displayed FISH signal.
source: Staining presented in an all or nothing fashion with 1085/1303 (83%) of larval stage animals, 317/326 (97%) of adult animals, and 50% of the embryos housed within uteri of adult animals displaying FISH signal (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental quantification.

claim: 97% of adult animals (317/326) displayed FISH signal.
source: Staining presented in an all or nothing fashion with 1085/1303 (83%) of larval stage animals, 317/326 (97%) of adult animals, and 50% of the embryos housed within uteri of adult animals displaying FISH signal (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental quantification.

claim: 50% of the embryos housed within uteri of adult animals displayed FISH signal.
source: Staining presented in an all or nothing fashion with 1085/1303 (83%) of larval stage animals, 317/326 (97%) of adult animals, and 50% of the embryos housed within uteri of adult animals displaying FISH signal (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental quantification.

claim: Out of 50 randomly chosen somatic nuclei, 50/50 had DNA FISH signal.
source: Out of 50 randomly chosen somatic nuclei 50/50 had DNA FISH signal.
evidence: This is supported by experimental quantification.

claim: 50/50 germline nuclei were positive for DNA FISH signals.
source: Likewise, 50/50 germline nuclei were positive for DNA FISH signals.
evidence: This is supported by experimental quantification.

claim: The library and hybridization strategy allows for robust and specific labeling of a whole chromosome in many cell types and many developmental stages simultaneously in large numbers of animals.
source: We conclude that our library and hybridization strategy allows for robust and specific labeling of a whole chromosome in many cell types and many developmental stages simultaneously in large numbers of animals.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: C. elegans chromosomes occupy largely distinct territories within interphase nuclei.
source: These data show that our DNA FISH approach is capable of labeling all six C. elegans chromosomes simultaneously in many different cell types of an intact animal. The data also show that, like interphase chromosomes in other eukaryotes, C. elegans chromosomes occupy largely distinct territories within interphase nuclei and that these chromosome territories persist in post-mitotic cells.
evidence: This is supported by the six chromosome FISH data showing distinct colored regions.

claim: C. elegans chromosome territories persist in post-mitotic cells.
source: These data show that our DNA FISH approach is capable of labeling all six C. elegans chromosomes simultaneously in many different cell types of an intact animal. The data also show that, like interphase chromosomes in other eukaryotes, C. elegans chromosomes occupy largely distinct territories within interphase nuclei and that these chromosome territories persist in post-mitotic cells.
evidence: This is supported by the observation of territories in somatic cells.

claim: Staining was robust, with 50/50 randomly chosen nuclei possessing all three fluorescent signals in successfully stained animals for 3 Mb and 500 kb subregion experiments.
source: Staining was robust, with 50/50 randomly chosen nuclei possessing all three fluorescent signals in successfully stained animals.
evidence: This is supported by experimental quantification.

claim: The Oligopaint library has the capability to visualize 3 Mb and 500 kb subregions of the C. elegans genome.
source: We conclude that the Oligopaint library has the capability to visualize 3 Mb and 500 kb subregions of the C. elegans genome.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing successful visualization of these subregions.

claim: Recent studies suggest that higher order chromatin structures may break down during aging, and in aging-related diseases such as Alzheimer's.
source: Recent studies suggest that higher order chromatin structures may break down during aging, and in aging-related diseases such as Alzheimer's (Winick-Ng and Rylett, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: Age-related alterations in nuclear morphology have been noted in C. elegans.
source: Age-related alterations in nuclear morphology have also been noted in C. elegans (Haithcock et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: In 10-day-old animals, chromosomes were no longer organized into discrete territories.
source: Interestingly, in 10-day-old animals, chromosomes were no longer organized into discrete territories (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: There was an ~50% increase in the volume of chromosomes I, II and III in aged animals compared to young animals.
source: Quantification (see Materials and methods) of the space occupied by chromosomes I, II and III in young and aged animals revealed an ~50% increase in the volume of all three chromosomes (Figure 5b)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 5b.

claim: There was an increase in the degree to which chromosomes I, II and III overlapped in subnuclear space in aged animals.
source: Quantification (see Materials and methods) of the space occupied by chromosomes I, II and III in young and aged animals revealed an ~50% increase in the volume of all three chromosomes (Figure 5b) as well as an increase in the degree to which chromosomes I, II and III overlapped in subnuclear space (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Chromosome territories did not become enlarged or disorganized in 10-day-old daf-2 mutant animals versus young animals.
source: Chromosome territories did not become enlarged or disorganized in 10-day-old daf-2 mutant animals versus young animals, indicating that the loss of chromosome territories we see in older wild-type animals is linked to aging and not chronological time (Figure 5a/b and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5a/b and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The loss of chromosome territories in older wild-type animals is linked to aging and not chronological time.
source: Chromosome territories did not become enlarged or disorganized in 10-day-old daf-2 mutant animals versus young animals, indicating that the loss of chromosome territories we see in older wild-type animals is linked to aging and not chronological time (Figure 5a/b and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison between wild-type and daf-2 mutant animals.

claim: daf-2 encodes an insulin-like receptor.
source: daf-2 encodes a insulin-like receptor and loss-of-function mutations in daf-2 and mutations in daf-2 such as e1370 cause animals to live twice as long as wild-type animals (Kenyon et al., 1993; Kimura et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations in daf-2 such as e1370 cause animals to live twice as long as wild-type animals.
source: daf-2 encodes a insulin-like receptor and loss-of-function mutations in daf-2 and mutations in daf-2 such as e1370 cause animals to live twice as long as wild-type animals (Kenyon et al., 1993; Kimura et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: mes-3 encodes a component of the Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2).
source: mes-3, which encodes a component of the Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2), was included in this small-scale screen because PRC2 is a known regulator of chromatin architecture in many organisms (Capowski et al., 1991; Holdeman et al., 1998; Ross and Zarkower, 2003; Xu et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: PRC2 is a known regulator of chromatin architecture in many organisms.
source: mes-3, which encodes a component of the Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2), was included in this small-scale screen because PRC2 is a known regulator of chromatin architecture in many organisms (Capowski et al., 1991; Holdeman et al., 1998; Ross and Zarkower, 2003; Xu et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: RNAi targeting mes-3 caused a loss of chromosome territories in adult hypodermal cells.
source: RNAi targeting mes-3 caused a loss of chromosome territories in adult hypodermal cells (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: There was an ~45% increase in chromosome volume in hypodermal nuclei when animals were exposed to mes-3 RNAi.
source: Quantification of chromosomes I, II, and III volumes in hypodermal nuclei revealed an ~45% increase in chromosome volume when animals were exposed to mes-3 RNAi, suggesting that MES-3 is important for maintaining chromosome territories of hypodermal cells during the normal course of growth and development (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 5d.

claim: MES-3 is important for maintaining chromosome territories of hypodermal cells during the normal course of growth and development.
source: Quantification of chromosomes I, II, and III volumes in hypodermal nuclei revealed an ~45% increase in chromosome volume when animals were exposed to mes-3 RNAi, suggesting that MES-3 is important for maintaining chromosome territories of hypodermal cells during the normal course of growth and development (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing increased chromosome volume after mes-3 RNAi.

claim: There was an ~2 fold increase in overlap of chromosomes I, II, and III after mes-3 RNAi.
source: Quantification of the degree to which DNA FISH signals for chromosomes I, II, and III overlapped revealed an ~2 fold increase in overlap after mes-3 RNAi, suggesting that chromosome territories are not just growing, they are also mixing (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: After mes-3 RNAi, chromosome territories are not just growing, they are also mixing.
source: Quantification of the degree to which DNA FISH signals for chromosomes I, II, and III overlapped revealed an ~2 fold increase in overlap after mes-3 RNAi, suggesting that chromosome territories are not just growing, they are also mixing (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is an inference based on the quantitative data showing increased overlap.

claim: MES-3 and PRC2 are needed to establish and/or maintain chromosome territories in C. elegans.
source: In summary, the data suggest that MES-3 and, therefore, PRC2 is needed to establish and/or maintain chromosome territories in C. elegans.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mes-3 RNAi experimental data.

claim: The invariant cell lineage, transparency, and small genome (100 Mb) of C. elegans make this animal an excellent system in which to explore how genome architecture relates to gene expression, development, growth, reproduction, and aging.
source: The invariant cell lineage, transparency, and small genome (100 Mb) of C. elegans make this animal an excellent system in which to explore how genome architecture relates to gene expression, development, growth, reproduction, and aging.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans as a model organism.

claim: DNA FISH experiments in C. elegans have historically relied on labeling PCR products that cover a single small (5–10 kb) region, or YACs to generate probes targeting larger regions (up to whole chromosomes).
source: DNA FISH experiments in C. elegans have historically relied on 1) labeling PCR products that cover a single small (5–10 kb) region, or 2) YACs to generate probes targeting larger regions (up to whole chromosomes).
evidence: This is established knowledge about historical DNA FISH methods in C. elegans.

claim: Most DNA FISH protocols rely on dissection of tissues, which is low throughput and limits the number of cell types that can be analyzed at one time.
source: Such experiments have also been limited by the types of cells that can be queried, as most DNA FISH protocols rely on dissection of tissues, which is low throughput and limits the number of cell types that can be analyzed at one time.
evidence: This is established knowledge about limitations of traditional DNA FISH protocols.

claim: The ability to rapidly and cheaply produce C. elegans DNA FISH probes, in conjunction with improvements to hybridization protocols, enables DNA FISH in all/most cells across all stages of development in an intact animal.
source: The ability to rapidly and cheaply produce C. elegans DNA FISH probes, in conjunction with improvements to hybridization protocols, enables DNA FISH in all/most cells across all stages of development in an intact animal.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data and methods developed in the study.

claim: Given the invariant cell lineage of C. elegans, it should now be possible to ask if chromosome-chromosome interactions or homolog pairing, or the size, morphology, or sub-nuclear positioning, of chromosomal territories (or subregions of these territories) vary predictably by cell type, age, or developmental trajectory.
source: Given the invariant cell lineage of C. elegans, it should now also be possible to ask if chromosome- chromosome interactions or homolog pairing, or the size, morphology, or sub-nuclear positioning, of chromosomal territories (or subregions of these territories) vary predictably by cell type, age, or developmental trajectory.
evidence: This is speculation about future research possibilities enabled by the developed methods.

claim: An Oligopaints bioinformatics pipeline was used to identify 42 bp DNA sequences in the C. elegans genome (genome reference Ce10) that uniquely map to the genome, exhibit similar melting temperatures and similar GC content, lack repetitive stretches, and lack predicted secondary structures.
source: An Oligopaints bioinformatics pipeline was used to identify 42 bp DNA sequences in the C. elegans genome (genome reference Ce10) that (1) uniquely map to the genome, (2) exhibit similar melting temperatures and similar GC content, (3) lack repetitive stretches, and (4) lack predicted secondary structures (Beliveau et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the methods used, supported by a citation.

claim: An updated bioinformatics pipeline for identifying probes is now available.
source: [Note, an updated bioinformatics pipeline for identifying probes is now available (Beliveau et al., 2018).]
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: Homologous chromosomes pair at the pachytene stage of Meiosis I at a defined region of the germline (termed pachytene region).
source: For instance, homologous chromosomes pair at the pachytene stage of Meiosis I at a defined region of the germline (termed pachytene region).
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans germline development.

claim: Oocytes are arrested in diakinesis of meiosis I and chromosomes are highly condensed with homologs connected via a single chiasmata (termed bivalents).
source: Oocytes are arrested in diakinesis of meiosis I and chromosomes are highly condensed with homologs connected via a single chiasmata (termed bivalents) (Villeneuve, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: Mature sperm harbor highly condensed chromosomes and are haploid.
source: Mature sperm harbor highly condensed chromosomes and are haploid.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans sperm.

claim: An alternative protocol allows for greater efficiency using isolated embryos (90%).
source: [Note, an alternative protocol that allows for greater efficiency using isolated embryos (90%) is described in Materials and methods.]
evidence: This is supported by the methods described in the manuscript.

claim: C. elegans typically live about 2 weeks.
source: We used our Oligopaint library to simultaneously visualize all six chromosomes in 1- and 10-day-old animals (C. elegans typically live about 2 weeks)
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans lifespan.

claim: In pachytene stage adult germ cells, C. elegans chromosomes are paired, condensed, and localized near the nuclear periphery.
source: In pachytene stage adult germ cells, C. elegans chromosomes are paired, condensed, and localized near the nuclear periphery (Albertson et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: The 170,594 sequences were ordered as two 90 k oligonucleotide chips from Custom Array (Bothell, WA).
source: The 170,594 sequences were ordered as two 90 k oligonucleotide chips from Custom Array (Bothell, WA).
evidence: This describes the methods used to obtain the oligonucleotide library.

claim: Each primary probe is 150 bp in length.
source: A series of barcode sequences were appended to each 42 bp hybridization sequence, which resulted in each primary probe being 150 bp.
evidence: This describes the design of the primary probes.

claim: Single stranded probe (primary probe) generation was conducted as previously described.
source: Single stranded probe (primary probe) generation was conducted as previously described (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the literature.
